title: Print the Elements of a Linked List
directAnswer: Walk a pointer from head to null, printing each node's value on its own line as you go. One while-loop, O(n) time, O(1) space. The only trap is the loop guard: stop when the pointer is null, and advance the pointer every iteration so you don't loop forever.

remember.pattern: Linear traversal: walk until null, visit each node
remember.formula:
cur = head
while cur is not None:
    print(cur.val)
    cur = cur.next
rules: Loop **while the pointer is not null**, not `while cur.next` — the latter skips the last node.
Advance `cur = cur.next` **inside** the loop on every iteration, or you spin forever on the head.
Use a **separate** pointer, not `head` itself — overwriting `head` loses the reference to the list.
An empty list (`head == null`) prints nothing — the loop body never runs, no special branch needed.
Print one value per line, in order from head to tail — don't reverse or collect-then-print unless asked.
whenToUse: You need to visit every node of a singly linked list exactly once
Reading / emitting list contents in head-to-tail order
Any base-case linked-list operation: counting, summing, searching, copying
Warm-up for harder traversals (reverse, cycle detection, merge)
antiSignals: You need the nodes in reverse order → reverse first, or recurse and print on the way back up
You must stop early at a condition → add the condition to the loop guard, don't print everything
You need random access by index → linked lists are O(n) per access; consider an array
remember.takeaway: The walk-until-null loop is the skeleton of every linked-list algorithm. Master the loop guard (`cur != null`) and the advance step (`cur = cur.next`), and harder problems become variations on this one shape.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you can write a clean traversal loop with the correct termination condition, advance the pointer every iteration, and not clobber the head reference.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Looping on `while cur.next` (drops the last node), forgetting `cur = cur.next` (infinite loop), or walking `head` directly so the list reference is lost.
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: State that it's O(n) time / O(1) space, that the empty list needs no special case, and that this loop is the template you'll reuse for count, search, and reverse.

problemStatement:
You are given the `head` of a singly linked list.

Print each element's value on its own line, in order from the head to the tail. If the list is empty, print nothing.

Return nothing — this is a side-effect (printing) task.
constraints: The list is singly linked (next pointers only)
understanding: Visit every node once, head to tail, emitting its value. Nothing is modified or returned — we only read and print. The list could be empty, in which case there is simply no output.

clarifyingQuestions.question: In what order should the values be printed?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Head to tail — the natural traversal order. Reversing would require extra work and isn't asked for.

clarifyingQuestions.question: What should happen for an empty list?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Print nothing. The traversal loop's body never executes when head is null, so no special branch is required.

clarifyingQuestions.question: One value per line, or separated some other way?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: One per line is the standard format for this problem. Confirm the separator if the spec is ambiguous.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Can I modify the list while printing?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: No need — printing is read-only. Use a separate traversal pointer and leave head untouched.

approaches.name: Iterative Traversal (Optimal)
approaches.whenToMention: This is the whole answer. Say it's O(n) time, O(1) space, and that the empty list falls out for free.
hints: You need to touch every node exactly once. What's the loop that walks a singly linked list from front to back?
Keep a pointer starting at head. While it isn't null, print its value, then move it to the next node.
What is the loop condition that includes the very last node but stops after it — `cur != null` or `cur.next != null`?
approaches.complexityReasoning: Each of the n nodes is visited and printed exactly once → O(n) time. A single pointer variable, no extra structures → O(1) space.
approaches.explanation:
Start a pointer `cur` at the head. While `cur` is not null, print `cur.val`, then advance `cur = cur.next`. When `cur` becomes null we've walked off the end and the loop stops.

**Why the guard is `cur != null`, not `cur.next != null`.** We want to print the *current* node, including the last one. The last node has `next == null` but is itself non-null, so `cur != null` prints it and *then* the advance makes `cur` null and ends the loop. If you guard on `cur.next != null`, the loop exits one node early and the tail never prints.

**Why advance every iteration.** The line `cur = cur.next` is what makes progress. Omit it and `cur` stays on the head forever — an infinite loop printing the same value. The advance must run on *every* pass, so it goes at the end of the loop body.

**Why a separate pointer.** We traverse with `cur`, not `head` itself. If you walk `head` to the end, you've lost your handle on the start of the list. Even though printing doesn't need head afterwards, using a dedicated pointer is the habit that keeps you safe in problems that do.

**Why the empty list needs no branch.** If `head` is null, `cur` starts null, the guard is immediately false, and the body never runs — printing nothing, which is exactly correct.
approaches.insight: This loop — initialise `cur = head`, guard `cur != null`, body then `cur = cur.next` — is the universal singly-linked-list traversal template. Counting nodes, summing values, searching for a key, and reversing all start from this exact skeleton; only the body changes.

pitfalls: Looping on `while cur.next != null` — drops the final node.
Forgetting `cur = cur.next` — infinite loop printing the head forever.
Walking `head` directly instead of a copy — loses the list reference for any later use.
Adding a special case for the empty list — the loop already handles it by printing nothing.

edgeCases.behavior: cur is null at the start; the loop body never runs; nothing is printed.
Prints 42, advances cur to null, loop ends. Single node works with no special handling.

commonMistakes: Using `while cur.next` as the guard, which skips printing the last node.
Forgetting to advance the pointer, causing an infinite loop on the head.
Traversing with `head` itself and losing the start-of-list reference.
Special-casing the empty list when the loop already prints nothing for it.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Wrong loop guard drops the last node
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Guarding on cur.next != null stops the loop while cur still points at the final node, so its value never prints. The guard must be on cur itself.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Forgetting to advance the pointer
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Without cur = cur.next, the pointer never moves off the head, so the guard stays true forever and the same value prints in an infinite loop.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad:
cur = head
while cur is not None:
    print(cur.val)
    # missing cur = cur.next -> infinite loop
commonMistakesDetailed.good:
cur = head
while cur is not None:
    print(cur.val)
    cur = cur.next

patternNote: The canonical singly-linked-list traversal: cur = head, while cur != null, advance cur = cur.next. Every count, search, sum, and reverse problem starts from this exact loop.
